scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9105: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports they have completely
lost connectivity to the partner network -- they cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2) in
the peer AS since this morning. The team is convinced the peer's router, router2,
dropped the peering and want router2 restarted. Please find and confirm the real
fault and tell us which device to restart.

injection.action: administratively down the inter-AS interface (eth0) on router1

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth0 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is the inter-AS link on router1: router1's eth0 (the interface to
router2) is DOWN, so the physical/L2 path between the two ASes is broken. As a
CONSEQUENCE the eBGP session between router1 and router2 drops and the inter-AS
prefixes are withdrawn, so pc1 (195.11.14.2) cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2). The
ticket MISDIRECTS to router2 ("router2 dropped the peering"), but the fault is on
the LOCAL side: it is router1's own inter-AS interface that is down. router2 is
healthy -- its bgpd is still running and its inter-AS interface is up; the session
is down only because router1's link went away.

The correct diagnosis identifies router1 (inter-AS link / eth0 down) as the root
cause and explicitly EXONERATES router2: router2's BGP daemon and interface are
fine, so the user's "router2 dropped the peering" hypothesis is wrong. An agent
that restarts / blames router2 has followed the ticket's misdirection instead of
the evidence.
scenario.fix_spec:
Bring the inter-AS link back up: on router1 run `ip link set eth0 up`. Once eth0
is up again, the eBGP session to router2 re-establishes, the inter-AS prefixes are
re-exchanged, and pc1 reaches pc2 normally. router2 needs no change -- it was
healthy the whole time.
scoring_axes: must-identify-link-down: identifies the inter-AS link (router1 eth0) is down as the root cause, with BGP loss as a consequence

bonus-notes-router2-healthy: rejects the ticket's "router2 dropped the peering" hypothesis by any valid evidence -- e.g. router2's config/daemon verified fine, its failed pings explained by the far end being down, or an explicit 'do not restart router2'

agent.diagnosis_text:
The failure is on router1’s inter-router interface (eth0), which is down at Layer 2. As a result, BGP cannot form from router1 to the peer, and router1 has no route to the partner network 200.1.1.0/24. That’s why pc1’s pings to pc2 elicit immediate “Destination Net Unreachable” messages sourced by 195.11.14.1 (router1): the router has no path to forward and returns an ICMP error.

Evidence:
- pc1 -> pc2 ping: “From 195.11.14.1 Destination Net Unreachable,” confirming router1 lacks a route.
- router1 routing table: only C 195.11.14.0/24; no 193.10.11.0/24 (interconnect) or 200.1.1.0/24 (peer LAN), matching a downed interconnect.
- router1 interface state: eth0 is DOWN (ip addr shows eth0 state DOWN; ifconfig flags lack UP/RUNNING).
- BGP on router1: neighbor 193.10.11.2 is “Active,” not established.
- router2 cannot reach 193.10.11.1 (Destination Host Unreachable), consistent with the far end interface being down.

Localization: router1, interface eth0 (193.10.11.1/24) toward router2. FRR on both routers is configured correctly; the control plane failure stems from the L2 interface state on router1.

Root cause: router1’s eth0 interface toward router2 is administratively or operationally down.

Corrective fix: Bring up router1’s eth0 (e.g., ip link set dev eth0 up or restart networking on router1). This will restore the interconnect, BGP adjacency will establish, and reachability to 200.1.1.0/24 will return. Do not restart router2; the issue is on router1.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly names router1's inter-AS interface (eth0) as down at L2 and states BGP loss is a consequence, matching the required root-cause identification.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-router2-healthy: rejects the ticket's "router2 dropped the peering" hypothesis by any valid evidence -- e.g. router2's config/daemon verified fine, its failed pings explained by the far end being down, or an explicit 'do not restart router2'
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly blames router1's eth0 (L2 down), shows router2's failures are explained by the far-end being down, notes FRR is fine on router2, and even advises not to restart router2.
Proposes bringing up router1's eth0 (e.g., ip link set dev eth0 up), which directly matches the expected remediation.

The checks cover interfaces, routing, BGP state, and directed pings, so the conclusion is well supported.
